newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to proceed with China rights resolution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to proceed with China rights resolution.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday said it would push forward with a U.N. resolution faulting China's human rights record despite Beijing's announced plans to sign an international covenant Washington encouraged.

"Frankly, we have not seen any significant change in the way China treats its people. Therefore, we are proceeding to support the resolution tabled by Denmark in Geneva at the U.N. Human Rights Comission," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

Burns, at a news briefing, said he had not been briefed by department experts on reports that China would sign the U.N. International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights and would check to "see if these reports are accurate."

But he stressed that even though Washington had pressed Beijing to sign the covenant, "more importantly we are looking for concrete pragmatic changes on the ground in China's human rights practices in the way that China treats its own population."

Burns said the United States hoped to defeat efforts by China to thwart debate on the resolution at the commission, now meeting in Geneva, and praised Denmark for taking the lead in sponsoring the resolution.

He said it was "unfortunate" that there were divisions in the European Union over the resolution, adding: "We certainly would have hoped the EU would speak with a single voice, a unified voice on this issue."

The EU divisions, coupled with the U.S. delay in deciding to co-sponsor the resolution until after Vice President Al Gore visited Beijing last week, makes it unlikely the resolution will be adopted, according to human rights activists.

China, a focus of controversy over its human rights record, has said it will sign the economic, social and cultural rights covenant but was silent on a similar pact on political freedoms, state media reported.

Beijing would sign the covenant before the end of the year and was now studying related domestic legislation, President Jiang Zemin told visiting French Defense Minister Charles Millon in a meeting on Monday.
"We evaluated the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights repeatedly," state media quoted Jiang as saying.
However, Jiang only said China would sign the first of the two covenants and made no further reference to the second, which the United States had also pressed Beijing to sign.

France hailed Chinese moves toward accepting United Nations human rights standards and said in a foreign ministry statement it hoped a European Union ban on arms sales to China imposed after the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown could be lifted.

In a thinly veiled attack on European partners who want the European Union to sponsor a U.N. resolution criticizing China's human rights record, the ministry said: "This decision is a signal which the international community must not ignore.
"It proves that a constructive, demanding dialogue which bears fruit is preferable to confrontation."

Before the U.N. commission meeting, the United States pressed China for concrete steps on human rights, including signing both covenants, releasing at least some key political prisoners and allowing the International Committee of the Red Cross to conduct prison visits.
If Beijing took such actions, officials said in February the United States was willing to drop its traditional support for the critical human rights resolution.

They indicated then that promising to sign the two covenants alone would not have been sufficient progress. But after Gore on his recent Beijing visit was criticized widely in the U.S. media for not taking as tough a stand toward China as House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, who also visited the city, it became impossible for the adminstration not to back the resolution strongly.
